doc.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022

chapter: Growing up and discovering Latin music
title: Concert halls, microphones and recording big bands
summary: Latin bands in sit-down halls, miking problems for percussion and horns, Machito's session setup and Yayo El Indio's voice.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Was it odd, later on, when a group like Mongo Santamaria, Tito Puente, if you put that group in Town Hall, at a sit down concert, did it change the music because there was no room for dancing? Now the audience is sitting and listening.

It didn’t change the music, but you could tell if the music was happening by people moving in their seats and occasionally getting up and being told by the ushers, sit down, you can’t do that here. We played, we did play a gig with Mongo’s band — I’m trying to think of where it was — a relatively well known concert hall. And the sound was terrible because they’re used to putting one microphone up in front of the orchestra, you know, the classical orchestra, and they balance themselves and they sound great. But in a band where you’ve got three percussionists that all play loud, you’ve got a timbale player, a conga player and a bongo player who also plays cowbell. It doesn’t work. So if they would put one microphone for them, naturally someone’s going to get lost in the mix. Same with the horns. If there’s one for the horns, someone’s going to get lost in the mix. So in those places, although prestigious, were not the best places to play.
Yeah that’s a great way for a brass player to blow their chops trying to play over the — I don’t know if there’s any such thing as a pianissimo timbale.

No. And you’re right about brass players. It was a struggle. As a matter of fact nowadays I see how everybody’s got a microphone. You know those clip on mics that they have for the horns and all? So you get a good soundman who gets a good sound balance on it, you can hear everything clearly. That’s a pleasure. But although I should say that there was some great big band recordings done with, for example I remember being at one session, I didn’t play on it but I was lucky enough to be there, Machito’s band recorded in a huge hall, it was a dance hall but in the daytime they would set up mics. And the way they would do it is the four trumpet players would set up in a circle and put a mic in the middle. The five sax players would set up in a circle and put a mic in the middle. And the producer, who is back in the booth, when they would do a test would say, “We need a little more alto sax” that meant moving your seat a little closer. Or, “We need a little less, we need a little more third trumpet, or a little less first trumpet” so everybody would © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

make that adjustment. But some of those albums sound great to this day, they really sound terrific. So technology offers the ability to do a lot of things that couldn’t be done, but that’s not to say that it’s better.
That’s a memorable statement. I mean I remember stories of Louis Armstrong had to move way back to the other end of the recording — the room where they were playing into a megaphone, right?

Yeah, yeah. It was a famous Latin vocalist named Yayo El Indio who had one of those voices. And when the singers would overdub the chorus parts they were also in a circle and Yayo was always told, “Stand back two steps” because he just had one of those voices that cut through.
